title: PHARMACOLOGY OF IOP-LOWERING AGENTS
summary: A comprehensive overview of the major pharmacological groups used to reduce intraocular pressure. This guide covers mechanisms of action, side effects, contraindications, and emerging therapeutic trends in glaucoma management.

sections.title: Modern Trends in Glaucoma Therapy
content: Increasing awareness of ocular side effects of preserved glaucoma drugs.
Focus on using preservative-free drop therapy.
Reducing polypharmacy by the use of fixed combination preparations.
Major drug groups summarized in table 10.6.

sections.title: Prostaglandin Analogues (PGAs)
sections.content:
These analogues of PGF2α increase uveoscleral outflow. 

• Ocular side effects: common—conjunctival hyperaemia, i pigmentation of iris (and sometimes lid skin), thickening and lengthening of lashes, loss of orbital fat; rare—uveitis, CMO, reactivation of herpetic kerato-uveitis.

sections.title: PGA Contraindications
content: May be associated with CMO after complicated cataract surgery (possibly active uveitis).

sections.title: Beta-blockers
sections.content:
These reduce aqueous production, probably by acting on β -receptors on the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium and vasoconstriction of the arterioles supplying ciliary processes. 

• Ocular side effects: uncommon; allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, punctate keratitis.

sections.title: Beta-blocker Red Flags
content: Asthma/COPD (bronchospasm may occur, even with selective β 1 agents)
Heart block
Bradycardia
Cardiac failure
Try to avoid in nursing mothers (secreted in breast milk)
Interaction: concurrent use of cardiac-directed Ca 2+ antagonists (e.g. verapamil) may compound bradycardia, heart block, and hypotension.

sections.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs)
sections.content:
These reduce aqueous production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase isoenzyme II (and hence bicarbonate production) in the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium. 

• Ocular side effects: common—burning, tearing, allergic blepharoconjunctivitis (up to 10%); rare—intraocular inflammation.

sections.title: CAI Contraindications & Interactions
content: Sulfonamide sensitivity
Renal failure
Liver failure (systemic acetazolamide)
Interaction: K+ -losing diuretics (e.g. thiazide) may cause profound hypokalaemia with acetazolamide.
Note: K+ supplementation is not usually required for acetazolamide used alone.

sections.title: Sympathomimetics
sections.content: The highly α2-selective brimonidine is well tolerated, and apraclonidine (α1 + α2) is useful for short-term use, e.g. after laser iridotomy. Non-selective sympathomimetics (adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrine, guanethidine) are now seldom used due to frequent side effects.

sections.title: Sympathomimetic Side Effects & Risks
content: Common: allergic blepharoconjunctivitis (15% brimonidine, 30% apraclonidine)
Older agents: scarring, mydriasis, adrenochrome deposits
Uncommon: CMO in aphakia (possibly pseudophakia)
Acute hypersensitivity: Intraocular inflammation and iIOP
Contraindications: heart block, bradycardia
Drug interactions: monoamine oxidase inhibitors

sections.title: Miotics (Parasympathomimetics)
sections.content:
Muscarinic receptor agonism leads to ciliary muscle contraction, which pulls on the scleral spur to open the trabecular meshwork. 

• Ocular side effects: fluctuating myopia, miosis (constricted VF, reduced night vision).

sections.title: Miotics: Clinical Use & Warnings
content: Pilocarpine: first line in narrow-angle glaucoma; sometimes in POAG.
Useful in: pigmentary glaucomas, aphakic glaucoma, some 2° glaucomas (e.g. post-PK).
Contraindications: inflammatory or aqueous misdirection/malignant glaucoma.
Systemic concern: GI disturbance.
